title: The Present Perfect
subtitle: Have you ever...? Experiences, news and results

say: I have found a secret map. Have you ever seen a glowing map? Mia is sharing news and asking about experiences. This is the present perfect.
It connects the past with now. Let's learn when to use it, how to make it, and how it is different from the past simple.

data.heading: Past action, present result
data.mark: I have lost my key. (I can't open the door now.)

say: The present perfect is a bridge between the past and now.
Something happened in the past, and we don't say exactly when.
What matters is the result now. I have lost my key. So I can't open the door now.

data.heading: Three main uses
examples: I <v>have been</v> to Muscat three times.
We <v>have lived</v> here for six years.
data.note: No finished time words like yesterday or in 2020.

say: There are three main uses.
Life experience: I have been to Muscat three times.
News, or a result you can see now: Whiskers has broken the cup!
And situations that started in the past and are still true: we have lived here for six years.
Remember: no finished time words like yesterday, or in twenty twenty.
Look! Whiskers has found the hidden path on the map. The line has started to glow.
beats.caption: Whiskers <v>has found</v> the hidden path.

say: The form: have or has, plus the past participle.
With I, you, we and they, use have, or the short form, apostrophe v e.
With he, she and it, use has, or apostrophe s.
I've seen it.
Mia's found a map.
Regular verbs end in e d, the same as the past simple: play, played, played.
But irregular verbs have their own form. Go, went, gone, or been.
See, saw, seen.
Eat, ate, eaten.
Write, wrote, written.
Find, found, found.
This third column is the one you need. Learn it with the verb.
A little trap: been or gone?
She has gone to Salalah means she is there now.
She has been to Salalah means she went there and came back. It's an experience.

data.heading: Questions and short answers
pairs: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.

say: For questions, put have or has first.
Have you ever ridden a camel? Yes, I have. Or, no, I haven't.
Has Mia finished her homework? Yes, she has.
How many times have you been there? Twice.
What have you done? I've broken the cup!

data.heading: Negative sentences
data.note: never = not ever: I've never seen snow.

say: For negatives, use haven't or hasn't.
I haven't seen that film.
She hasn't called me.
We can also use never: we've never been to Paris.
Never already means not, so don't say I haven't never.

data.heading: Time words with the present perfect

say: Some words love the present perfect.
Just means a moment ago: I've just eaten. Already means sooner than expected: she's already finished.
Yet goes at the end of questions and negatives: have you finished yet? I haven't finished yet. Ever is used in questions about life, and never in negatives.
For is a period: for three years. Since is the starting point: since twenty twenty, since Monday, since I was six.

data.heading: Present perfect or past simple?
rows: She lost it at school on Monday.

say: When do we use the past simple instead? When we say, or know, the finished time.
I've visited Nizwa, an experience. But: I visited Nizwa last year.
Have you seen my bag? But: did you see it yesterday?
She's lost her phone. But: she lost it at school on Monday.

data.heading: Common mistakes (Arabic speakers)
rows: I am here for two years.
I have been here for two years.

say: Now the common mistakes.
I have seen him yesterday. Yesterday is finished, so: I saw him yesterday.
I live here since twenty nineteen. With since, use the present perfect: I have lived here since twenty nineteen.
She has went home. Use the participle: she has gone home.
Did you ever eat sushi? For life experience: have you ever eaten sushi?
I am here for two years. Say: I have been here for two years.

lines: Have you ever been to Salalah?
We've lived here for six years.

data.heading: The secret box
data.sub: Listen for have, has, just and never

say: A short story. Listen for have, has, just and never.
Mia has opened Grandma's old box. Someone has drawn a picture of a girl and a black cat. Mia has never seen it before.
beats.caption: Someone <v>has drawn</v> a girl and a cat.

say: And Whiskers? Whiskers has just fallen asleep, next to the glowing map. It has been a long day.
beats.caption: Whiskers <v>has just fallen</v> asleep.

data.heading: Your turn!
data.sub: Pause the video if you need more time

say: Quiz time. Five questions. You have five seconds each.

data.q: She ___ her keys. She can't get in.

beats.say_answer: Has lost. She is he, she, it, so has.
Saw. Last week is finished time, so past simple.
Since. Twenty nineteen is the starting point.
Yet. In questions and negatives, yet goes at the end.

data.q: He has ___ to Salalah. He's there now.

beats.say_answer: Gone. He is still there now.

data.heading: Remember
items: Past action, result or experience now
Learn the third form: seen, gone, eaten
been = went and came back; gone = still there
just, already, yet, ever, never, for, since

say: Let's remember. The present perfect connects the past with now: experiences, news and results.
Have or has, plus the past participle. And learn the third form of irregular verbs.
Use it with just, already, yet, ever, never, for and since. But with a finished time, like yesterday, use the past simple.
